stories.title: Detroit’s Seniors Joined a Time Bank For Help. They Became Its Biggest Helpers.
stories.summary: In Southwest Detroit, seniors joined a time bank for help with rides and porch repairs — then became its most active helpers. The Unity in Our Community TimeBank has 842 members and logged about 1,000 exchanges in the last year, turning neighbors into a support system.
stories.extended_summary: Nearly 55% of Detroit seniors live alone, many in aging homes with loose porch steps and no easy ride to the doctor. Asking a neighbor for help can feel like too much — so the Unity in Our Community TimeBank built a system where asking is the point. Members earn credits by helping others, then spend them on the help they need. Founded in 2009, the Southwest Detroit time bank now has 842 members and logged roughly 1,000 exchanges in the past year. The surprise? Seniors who joined looking for assistance became the network's biggest contributors. It's a quiet rebuttal to the idea that older adults are only on the receiving end — and proof that connection, not charity, is what actually sustains a community.

stories.extended_summary: By 9 a.m. on opening day, about 30 students had already walked into Kingdom Café — most with no money, all looking for somewhere safe before the school bell rang. The café sits inside the MLK Wellness Center, a South Dallas hub developer Ferrell Fellows first envisioned in 2023 and predicted would take 18 months to build. It took more than four years, through permitting delays, aging infrastructure, and ballooning construction costs. What finally opened is more than a building: it's healthy food, fitness, and mental health services for a neighborhood that's been waiting a long time for someone to follow through.

stories.summary: Evan Newton, 25, bought the weekly Monticello News — the paper he used to intern at — and made himself editor and publisher. Six weeks in, he'd grown print and digital subscriptions 30 percent, partly by posting paper summaries on TikTok.
stories.extended_summary: Evan Newton announced it on TikTok: "I'm a twenty-five-year-old who just bought my local newspaper, and here's my first edition." The video racked up more than 5,600 views — nearly triple the Monticello News' entire print circulation of about 2,000 across Jasper County, Georgia. Six weeks after buying the weekly paper where he'd once interned, Newton had grown print and digital subscriptions 30 percent, largely by posting summaries on TikTok to reach people his age who'd stopped picking up print. He's the paper's only full-time employee, working out of a small red house off the town square as reporter, opinion columnist, and designer. A teen recently told him at a football game: "I didn't even know Monticello had a paper, and now I'm trying to get one every week."

stories.extended_summary: David Clarke estimates it will take him three to five years to clean up every forgotten tree bed, underpass, and planter in New York City. The 24-year-old Washington Heights resident has already made a big dent in his own neighborhood, and now he's using his rapidly growing TikTok and Instagram accounts to teach his 8.5 million neighbors how to beautify the city themselves. Clarke calls it reversing 'learned helplessness'—the idea that people rely too much on the government to maintain public spaces. He's planted seasonal flora, built benches for neighbors with mobility issues, and shoveled out overgrown weeds. In just five months, he's amassed over 230,000 followers and fundraised for more trash cleanup. 'This only makes sense if you view it as something I do from 7 a.m. to the moment I go to sleep every day,' he says.

stories.summary: A growing number of US courtrooms are being redesigned for Indigenous child welfare cases — with cedar oil, sweetgrass, and judges sitting at round tables instead of benches. The goal: keep Native kids connected to their tribes.

stories.summary: A 16-year-old public/private preschool partnership in Auburn, Nebraska got the spotlight at a statewide early childhood conference. Born from a simple need — more preschool spots, no space to put them — the Little Learners model is now the only one of its kind in the state, and it's still going strong.
stories.extended_summary: "We weren't trying to create an innovative model. We were trying to solve a problem." That's how Deb Reiman describes the partnership she started 16 years ago when Auburn needed more preschool seats but the school district had no room, no staff, and no transportation to make it happen. The solution: a privately owned preschool taught by a certified teacher, supported by the district with a paraeducator, screenings, and state aid for eligible four-year-olds. It's still the only public/private preschool model operating in Nebraska. This September, Reiman and her partners shared the story at the Thriving for Children Conference in Kearney, showing early childhood professionals from across the state how a workaround became a blueprint.

This is the 22nd consecutive year of the Lesser Scaup Project, one of the longest-running and most detailed datasets on breeding ducks anywhere in the world. The Red Rock Lakes National Wildlife Refuge, the largest wetland complex in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, hosts thousands of migratory birds. While the refuge was created to protect trumpeter swans, the scaup has become its quiet conservation story — tracked one banded bird at a time.

stories.title: Energy Dome and its carbon dioxide batteries
stories.summary: Energy Dome is storing renewable power in giant domes of compressed carbon dioxide, delivering up to 24 hours of grid backup. It's a clever fix for the biggest weakness of solar and wind: they don't always show up.
stories.extended_summary: Picture a white dome the size of seven soccer fields, holding 2,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide — and using it as a battery. Energy Dome compresses CO2 into liquid when solar or wind power is plentiful, storing the heat generated along the way. When the grid needs juice, the gas is released, warmed, and pushed through a turbine to make electricity. Unlike compressed-air storage that needs underground caverns, this works anywhere. As renewables strain to meet rising demand, it's a promising answer to the intermittency problem.
